What temperature do Venus flytraps like in summer?

Anywhere from about 20 to 35 degrees Celsius suits them, and they are happiest at the warm end with strong sun. They tolerate short spells above 35 provided the roots stay wet and cool, which is why keeping the tray topped up matters more than shading the leaves. Growth slows below about 10 degrees. Cold is only wanted in winter, when dormancy needs roughly 0 to 10 degrees.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How hot is too hot for a Venus flytrap?

Sustained air temperatures above about 35 degrees Celsius start to stress them, and above 38 you will see limp leaves and browning tips. The danger is rarely the air itself - it is hot, dry roots. Keep the tray deeper than usual in a heatwave and shade the pot rather than the plant, since cooling the root zone is what actually helps. They recover well once it passes.

How cold can a Venus flytrap get during the growing season?

Nights down to about 5 degrees Celsius are harmless during spring and autumn, and a light frost will not kill an established plant, though it will push it toward dormancy. What you want to avoid is prolonged cold in midsummer, which simply stops growth. Consistent nights below 10 degrees are the plant's signal that the season is ending.

What temperature range do Sarracenia want?

Roughly 20 to 35 degrees Celsius through the growing season, and they are among the most heat-tolerant carnivorous plants - a hot southern summer suits them well as long as they are standing in water. Growth is best with warm days and cooler nights. In winter they need the opposite: about three months near or just above freezing.

How cold hardy are Sarracenia?

It varies by species. S. purpurea is the toughest and survives hard freezes well below minus 10 degrees Celsius in the ground, and S. flava and S. oreophila are also very hardy. The Gulf coast species such as S. leucophylla and S. psittacina are less so and want protection below about minus 5. In pots, any of them is more vulnerable than in the ground because the whole root ball can freeze solid.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What temperature does a Nepenthes need?

It depends on whether it is a lowland or highland species, which is the single most important thing to know about a Nepenthes. Lowlanders want 25 to 35 degrees Celsius by day and 20 to 25 at night. Highlanders want 20 to 28 by day but 10 to 16 at night, and they genuinely need that drop. Intermediate hybrids like N. ventrata are forgiving of anything between.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What night temperature do highland Nepenthes actually need?

Around 10 to 16 degrees Celsius, and the drop from daytime matters as much as the number - a swing of roughly 10 degrees between day and night is what these plants evolved with on tropical mountains. Without it they survive but grow slowly and often stop pitchering. A room that sits at a constant 22 degrees all day and night is the classic reason a highland species sulks.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is my house at a constant 21 degrees suitable for carnivorous plants?

It suits subtropical and intermediate plants well - Cape sundew, D. spatulata, Mexican butterworts and intermediate Nepenthes such as N. ventrata will all grow happily at a steady 21 degrees given enough light. It does not suit highland Nepenthes, which need cool nights, or temperate species like flytraps and Sarracenia, which need somewhere cold for winter.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What temperature suits a Cape sundew?

It is comfortable anywhere from about 15 to 30 degrees Celsius, which is why it is such a good indoor plant - ordinary room temperature is fine year round. It tolerates cooler conditions down to a few degrees above freezing and will slow but not die. Hard frost damages it, so if it summers outdoors bring it in before the first freeze.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What temperatures do Mexican butterworts want?

Roughly 15 to 30 degrees Celsius during the sticky summer phase, and cooler through the winter succulent phase, ideally around 10 to 20 with much less water. They dislike sustained heat above about 32 combined with wet roots, which is when rot tends to set in. A normal room suits them well, which is part of why they are good beginner plants.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What temperature does Cephalotus prefer?

About 20 to 28 degrees Celsius by day with a drop into the mid-teens at night. It comes from a Mediterranean climate in southwest Australia, so it dislikes sustained heat above roughly 35 and appreciates cooler winters without a hard freeze. Good air movement matters more for this species than for most, since warm still air encourages rot.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What temperatures do Heliamphora need?

They are highland plants from the tepuis, so about 20 to 25 degrees Celsius by day and 10 to 15 at night, with the night drop being essential rather than optional. They also want very high humidity. This combination of cool nights and constant humidity is exactly why they are considered advanced - most homes provide neither without a dedicated chamber.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Does Darlingtonia really need cold roots, and how cold?

Yes. It grows in mountain seeps fed by cold running water, so it wants root temperatures below roughly 25 degrees Celsius even when the air is warm. The air can be hot without harm. Growers manage it by flushing the pot with cold mineral-free water on hot days, growing in a large pot that heats slowly, or shading the pot while leaving the foliage in sun.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do carnivorous plants need a day and night temperature difference?

Most benefit from one but only highland species genuinely require it. Highland Nepenthes and Heliamphora need a drop of about 10 degrees Celsius at night to grow and pitcher properly. Temperate plants like flytraps and Sarracenia get this naturally outdoors and do not need it engineered. Lowland Nepenthes are content with warm nights.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is the temperature of the soil different from the air temperature?

It can be, and it matters. A black plastic pot in direct summer sun can run well above air temperature, cooking the roots while the leaves look fine - which is why heat damage often shows up as wilting in a plant that is standing in water. Keeping the tray topped up buffers this, and shading just the pot is more effective than shading the whole plant.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Does a windowsill get too hot behind glass?

It can. Glass traps heat, so a south-facing sill in summer can sit 10 degrees above room temperature and dry a small pot out within hours. The plants themselves tolerate the heat; the risk is the pot running dry. Use a deeper tray in summer, or move the plant outdoors, which gives better light and more stable temperatures at once.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What temperature should I germinate seed at?

Around 20 to 25 degrees Celsius for most species once any cold stratification is finished. Warmth plus light plus constant moisture is the combination. Nepenthes and other tropical seed prefer the warmer end, closer to 25 to 28. Temperate seed that has been through its cold period germinates readily at normal room temperature in spring.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
My greenhouse hits 40 degrees in summer. Is that a problem?

For temperate bog plants it is survivable but not ideal, and it becomes dangerous if the trays run dry. Add shading and ventilation, keep water levels deep, and expect growth to stall during the hottest spells. Sarracenia cope best. Nepenthes highland species and Cephalotus will suffer at that temperature and are better moved somewhere cooler.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is a cold night going to hurt my plants in autumn?

For temperate species, no - cool autumn nights are the cue that starts dormancy and are exactly what you want. For tropical plants it is a different matter: bring Nepenthes and other tropicals indoors before nights fall below about 12 to 15 degrees Celsius. The mistake is treating both groups the same when the seasons turn.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What is the minimum temperature for a Nepenthes?

Most tropical Nepenthes start to suffer below about 12 to 15 degrees Celsius, with lowland species being the most sensitive. Brief dips are survivable but sustained cold causes leaf drop and rot. Highland species tolerate the low end comfortably, since cool nights are what they want, but even they should not be exposed to frost.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can carnivorous plants live in an air-conditioned room?

Yes, though air conditioning dries the air and holds temperatures very steady, which suits subtropical plants better than highland ones. The bigger practical issue is that a constant temperature removes the day-night swing highland Nepenthes need. Keep plants out of the direct draught, since a cold dry airstream will crisp leaf tips.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Do temperate plants need warm summers to be healthy?

They benefit from them. Flytraps and Sarracenia produce their largest traps and pitchers in warm, bright conditions, and a cool cloudy summer generally means smaller growth. It is not a health problem, just a smaller plant. The pairing that matters is a warm growing season followed by a genuinely cold winter - both halves of the cycle.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What ratio of peat to sand should I use?

One to one by volume is the standard mix for flytraps, Sarracenia and most sundews - equal parts sphagnum peat and washed silica sand. Some growers go a little heavier on peat, around two parts peat to one of sand, which holds more water. Either works. What matters far more is that both ingredients are plain and additive-free, and that the sand is silica rather than builders or beach sand.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What ratio should I use if I am using perlite instead of sand?

Two parts peat to one part perlite is a good general mix, or one to one if you want it more open. Perlite is lighter than sand, so a pot mixed with it floats and shifts more in a tray, which some growers dislike. Rinse it before use. You can also combine all three - two parts peat, one sand, one perlite - which is a solid all-purpose bog mix.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What mix ratio do Nepenthes want?

Pure long fibre sphagnum is the simplest and works very well. If you prefer a blend, try roughly three parts sphagnum to one part perlite and one part orchid bark, which stays open and drains fast. The principle is that Nepenthes are epiphytic or semi-epiphytic and hate a dense waterlogged mix, unlike your bog plants.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How much perlite is too much?

Beyond about half the volume the mix stops holding enough water for bog plants and the pot dries out between top-ups. For flytraps and Sarracenia, keep perlite to a third or less of the total. Nepenthes are the exception and tolerate much more, since they want an airy mix. If your pot is drying out faster than the tray empties, there is too much.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What mix do Mexican butterworts want and in what proportion?

More mineral than most - roughly equal parts peat, washed sand and perlite, and many growers add pumice or fine gravel to push it further. Some use almost no peat at all. The reason is that Mexican pings grow on limestone in the wild and dislike a soggy peat-heavy mix, particularly during their winter succulent phase when they want to be barely moist.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How close should a grow light be to the plants?

For a typical LED panel, 20 to 30 centimetres above the plants is a good starting point. Closer gives more intensity but risks heat and bleaching; further loses intensity quickly, since light falls off with the square of distance. Judge by the plants rather than the tape measure: compact leaves with red colour means it is right, stretching means lower it.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What light intensity are carnivorous plants actually after?

In proper units, aim for roughly 200 to 400 micromoles per square metre per second at plant level for sun-loving species, which works out to a daily light integral of about 15 to 25 moles per square metre per day over a 14 hour photoperiod. Full summer sun outdoors is well above that. Shade species like D. adelae are happy at a fraction of it.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How many watts of LED do I need?

Wattage is a poor guide because efficiency varies so much between fixtures, but as a rough starting point a 30 to 50 watt modern LED panel will light a shelf around 60 by 30 centimetres well enough for flytraps and sundews. Look for a stated photosynthetic photon flux figure if the manufacturer gives one, and otherwise judge by how the plants grow over a few weeks.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How many hours a day should the light be on?

Twelve to fourteen hours during the growing season is the usual range, set on a timer so it is consistent. Fourteen suits sun-loving species well. For temperate plants being overwintered under lights, cut to eight to ten hours or switch off entirely, since a long photoperiod works against the dormancy you are trying to induce.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I use a lux meter or a phone app to check my light?

You can, as a rough guide. Aim for something above 10,000 lux at plant level for sun-loving species, with full outdoor sun being 100,000 or more. The caveat is that lux is weighted for human vision rather than photosynthesis, so it undervalues red and blue light and will read low under a magenta grow light. Treat it as a relative comparison, not an absolute.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can a plant get too much light?

Rarely from intensity alone - these are full-sun plants - but a sudden change will scorch them, which is why a plant moved from indoors to full sun bleaches within days. The other real limit is heat: intense light close to a plant in a still, enclosed space cooks it. Increase exposure over a week or two and keep air moving.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What TDS reading should I aim for?

Under 50 parts per million is the usual target, and under 20 is better. Distilled and reverse osmosis water typically read close to zero, and clean rainwater is usually under 20. Tap water commonly runs 150 to 400 or higher. A cheap TDS meter takes the guesswork out of judging whether a filter jug or a bottled water is actually suitable, and they usually are not.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How deep should the water in the tray be?

One to two centimetres for most of the growing season, topped up when it runs dry. Deeper is fine in a heatwave and helps buffer against a pot drying out. In winter keep it shallower, or let the tray empty between top-ups, because cold plus permanently sodden soil is what causes rot. Never fill the tray more than about a third of the pot height.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How often should I feed my plants and how much?

For an indoor plant during the growing season, one or two traps or leaves every one to two weeks is plenty - there is no need to feed every trap. Use prey that fits comfortably inside the trap, roughly a third of its size. Outdoor plants need no feeding at all. Never feed a dormant plant, and never put fertiliser in the soil.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How long should dormancy last, exactly?

About three months is the standard, and 10 to 14 weeks is the practical range for flytraps and Sarracenia. Shorter than about ten weeks and the plant does not get the full benefit; longer does no harm. What matters alongside duration is the temperature - broadly 0 to 10 degrees Celsius - and that the medium stays damp but not sodden throughout.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What size pot should I use and how deep?

Depth matters more than width for most of these plants. Flytraps and Sarracenia send roots down, so aim for at least 12 to 15 centimetres deep, and 20 or more for a mature Sarracenia. Pygmy sundews want a surprisingly deep pot for their size because of their long tap root. Width follows the plant: allow a few centimetres around a clump for a season or two of growth.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How often should I repot?

Every one to two years for most species, in early spring. The peat breaks down over time into a dense airless sludge, which is the real reason for repotting rather than the plant outgrowing the pot. Nepenthes in sphagnum can go two to three years. If growth has slowed and the mix feels compacted rather than springy, it is due.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How long does seed take to come up?

Two to five weeks for fresh flytrap seed, two to six weeks for Sarracenia after stratification, two to four weeks for subtropical sundews, and one to three months for Nepenthes. Stragglers keep appearing for months afterwards, so do not throw a seed pot out early. Old seed is much slower and much less reliable, which is why fresh sowing matters.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How many leaf pullings can I take from one plant at once?

Two or three from a healthy mature flytrap in spring, no more. Each pulling is a leaf the plant loses, so stripping a plant weakens it for the season and gains you little, since success rates are middling anyway. Take a few, let the parent recover through summer, and take more the following spring.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How many plants would I need to control fungus gnats in a room?

A few butterworts or sundews positioned near the source will noticeably reduce the population, but no realistic number of plants eliminates an established infestation on their own. They are a useful trap for the adults; the larvae are in the soil of your houseplants, which is what actually needs addressing. Treat the plants as monitoring and suppression, not eradication.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How much water should I give a Nepenthes and how often?

Water from the top until it drains freely from the bottom, then let the surface of the mix become just barely dry before watering again - typically every two to four days indoors depending on warmth and pot size. Unlike your bog plants they should not sit permanently in a tray. Use the same mineral-free water as everything else.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How long until a cutting roots?

Nepenthes stem cuttings usually take six to twelve weeks in damp sphagnum at high humidity, and it is normal to see nothing for the first month. Sundew leaf cuttings show plantlets in three to six weeks. Flytrap leaf pullings take one to three months. Root cuttings are often quicker than leaf cuttings for the sundews that take them.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How big should the insect be that I feed my flytrap?

About a third of the trap's length, so that the trap can seal completely around it. Anything protruding stops the seal forming, which lets the catch rot and usually blackens the trap. For a typical 3 centimetre trap that means something around a centimetre - a small fly, a young cricket, or a pinch of rehydrated bloodworm rather than one large insect.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How many hours of direct sun does a flytrap need as a minimum?

Four hours of genuine direct sunlight is the practical minimum, and six or more gives noticeably better results - shorter leaves, larger traps and strong red colour. Bright indirect light does not count, however bright the room looks to you. If your window cannot deliver four hours, use a grow light rather than hoping.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
How much does light drop off if I raise the lamp?

Sharply - intensity falls with the square of the distance, so doubling the height from 25 to 50 centimetres leaves roughly a quarter of the light at plant level. This is why small changes in lamp height make a much bigger difference than people expect, and why raising a light to cover more plants quietly starves all of them.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
What proportion of sand should a pygmy sundew mix have?

Sandier than a standard bog mix - equal parts peat and washed silica sand at minimum, and many growers go further, to two parts sand to one of peat. They still want the pot standing in water; the sand is about structure rather than drainage. Use a deep pot despite their tiny size, since they send down a long tap root.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Can I use 100% sphagnum moss with no peat at all?

Yes, for many plants. Pure long fibre sphagnum suits Nepenthes, Heliamphora, cuttings and seedlings very well, and live sphagnum works for shade-loving sundews. For flytraps and Sarracenia a peat and sand mix is more usual and cheaper, but pure sphagnum will grow them perfectly well. Just make sure it is plain horticultural sphagnum with nothing added.
You are a knowledgeable assistant that answers questions about caring for carnivorous plants.
Is there a number I should aim for with humidity?

For flytraps, Sarracenia and most sundews, no - they grow fine at ordinary household humidity of 40 to 50 percent and do not need any intervention. Nepenthes prefer 60 percent or above, and highland species and Heliamphora want 70 or more. Chasing humidity for temperate plants is one of the most common wasted efforts in this hobby.
